Prescind means to deliberately set something aside in your mind — to consciously choose to leave something out of your thinking so you can focus more clearly on something else.

The crucial thing to understand is that you are not saying the thing you're setting aside is unimportant or nonexistent. You're saying: "For the purposes of what I'm currently thinking about, I'm going to mentally step past this." It is a careful, purposeful act of intellectual separation.
The Pattern You'll Almost Always See

Prescind almost always appears as "prescind from [something]" — you prescind from the thing you're setting aside.

Here are some examples:

  • "Let us prescind from questions of cost for now and decide whether the plan is actually feasible."
  • "Prescinding from the political complications, the policy itself is well-designed."
  • "The philosopher asked us to prescind from our emotions and reason about the problem purely in logical terms."

In every case, the person isn't denying those things exist or matter. They're making a deliberate choice to mentally park them to one side.

Think of a spotlight in a dark room. You know there are other things in the room — furniture, people, objects — but you are deliberately directing the light onto just one thing. To prescind from everything else is to consciously choose not to shine the light on those other things right now. They're still there. You just aren't examining them in this moment.

Occasionally, you'll see "prescind" used slightly differently, where you prescind one thing from another — meaning you mentally detach something from its usual context to consider it in pure isolation.

For example: "He prescinded the idea of justice from its social context and examined it in the abstract."

Here, justice is being mentally cut away from everything surrounding it, so it can be looked at on its own terms. This use is less common, but the core idea is the same: a deliberate act of intellectual separation.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay attention here.

Ignore carries a negative flavor — it implies carelessness, negligence, or even disrespect. Prescind is entirely neutral. You're not being careless; you're making a rigorous intellectual choice. A scholar who prescindsfrom something is being more careful, not less.

Disregard has a similarly dismissive tone. The thing you prescind from may be enormously important — you're just choosing not to factor it into this particular line of thinking.

Bracket (as used in academic or philosophical discussion — "let's bracket that issue") is the closest everyday equivalent. Prescind is simply the more formal, precise version of this.

Abstract means something different: to pull a general idea out of specific examples. Prescind is not about extracting — it's about excluding from consideration.

Prescind is rare in everyday conversation. You'll find it mainly in philosophy and theology (its most natural home), academic writing, formal legal arguments, and policy discussions. When you do encounter it, the context will almost always be someone making a careful intellectual argument who wants to temporarily narrow the scope of consideration.
The One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Whenever you see "prescind from X", translate it mentally as: deliberately setting X aside in order to think more clearly about something else. That is the word's entire job, and everything else above is just the nuance around that core idea.
